messages.body_plain:
Dear Dr Jefferis,

Apologies for the lack of clarity.  My issue is that the position of flycircuit neurons relative to both my tracing and the FCWB brain rendering is different when these neurons are visualised using plot3d vs when visualised using the NBLAST GUI, as can be seen in the images below. At point A in the NBLAST gui my tracing almost perfectly maps onto the red and orange neuron, however when these same neurons are visualised with plot3d there is a large gap between them. At point B in the plot3d() rendering the green neuron pokes out of the brain significantly more than it is shown to in the NBLAST gui rendering, as if it is shifted down. My search parameters were: fcwb template + mirror + compare with all neurons.

With regards to the lines joining tracing ends, I have attached a sample trace which gets distorted by the end joining effect. No such end-joining appears when visualised using the plot3d() function however.

Thank you again for your time.

George.

I'm afraid I don't fully understand your question. Is it that you get a high NBLAST score but then the neurons don't look identical? I would need more specifics to comment. What was your query? What were your search parameters. Were you using forward or mean score?

However looking at your attached images, the black trace is a good matche for some of those neurons – the neurons just have more processes. But that is to be expected, your tracing is highly simplified and no real neuron looks like that.

Re your second question about the line joining the ends of the tracing, you would have to send a sample file. I have not seen this before, so there must be something relatively specific about your tracing.

Best wishes,

Greg.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Emil,

I'm glad to hear that the live synaptic connectivity information has been useful. When you run a query in fafbseg, it fetches the data from a microservice run by Eric Perlman on behalf of the BRAIN initiative grant awarded to Davi Bock and myself. We haven't really advertised it too heavily, because stimulated by our implementation (and with some input from us) the flywire team have been working on their own implementation which should be more efficient and integrated. I don't know when to expect that because they are working on a number of other related enhancements, but it should be soon.

The neurotransmitter prediction is still very experimental – Nils Eckstein in Jan Funke's lab only ran the whole brain predictions a month ago – but Jan and I agreed that the results should be made available to the flywire community as soon as possible and so we have given the information to Sven Dorkenwald and colleagues to integrate with the flywire synapse service that I mention above.

Should it take more than a week or so for this synapse information to appear via flywire, we can arrange a workaround using the same database microsevice that powers the synapse queries you are running from fafbseg.

All the best,

Greg.

messages.subject_clean: Distribution of a neuron across each neuropil
messages.body_plain:
Hi natverse team,

I was hoping to use your powerful suite of R packages to analyze the data released by FlyCircuit, and would greatly appreciate any help with regards to a few questions that I have.

1. I was wondering why the template flybrain (e.g., plot3d(FCWP)) looks squished front-to-back? Are the coordinates not isometric? I want to make sure that I am not doing something wrong.

2. Given a FlyCircuit neuron, I want its distribution across each neuropil region (FCWBNP.surf$RegionList), i.e., the overlapping voxel count of the neuron per neuropil region. This voxel count is provided for 16129 neurons in the dataset http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/si/nblast/flycircuit/dpscanon.rds, but how can I calculate this for a new (not included in the dataset) neuron scraped from the FlyCircuit website?

While the voxel counts would be ideal, I suspect it would also be sufficient for my purposes to instead just get a distribution of the segment lengths (of the neuron) in each neuropil region. Below is the sequence of steps that I have been able to successfully implement so far:
fc_read_neurons() - to scrape a neuron from the FlyCircuit website.
xform_brain() - to register the neuron into FCWP space.
prune_in_volume() - to obtain a break-up of the number of vertices and segments present in each neuropil region.
However, I am unsure of how to proceed next. How can I calculate the segment lengths, and ultimately determine what proportion of the neuron is present in each neuropil?

Thank you for your help.

Ketan Mehta, PhD
--
Postdoctoral Research Fellow
The Center for Neural Informatics, Neural Structures, and Neural Plasticity
Bioengineering Department, Volgenau School of Engineering
George Mason University, MS2A1, Fairfax, VA 22030 (USA)

Dear Ketan,

Thanks for your interest in the natverse.

> 1. I was wondering why the template flybrain (e.g., plot3d(FCWP)) looks squished front-to-back? Are the coordinates not isometric? I want to make sure that I am not doing something wrong.

This is an artefact of the imaging by the flycircuit.tw <http://flycircuit.tw> team. Although their images are of high quality (with one of our best ever registration success rates) there must be an uncorrected refractive index mismatch since the brain should be at least 50% larger in Z real life.

> 2. Given a FlyCircuit neuron, I want its distribution across each neuropil region (FCWBNP.surf$RegionList), i.e., the overlapping voxel count of the neuron per neuropil region. This voxel count is provided for 16129 neurons in the dataset http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/si/nblast/flycircuit/dpscanon.rds, but how can I calculate this for a new (not included in the dataset) neuron scraped from the FlyCircuit website?

While the voxel counts would be ideal, I suspect it would also be sufficient for my purposes to instead just get a distribution of the segment lengths (of the neuron) in each neuropil region. Below is the sequence of steps that I have been able to successfully implement so far:
fc_read_neurons() - to scrape a neuron from the FlyCircuit website.
xform_brain() - to register the neuron into FCWP space.

By default fc_read_neurons transforms neurons into FCWB space so you do not need to do this yourself.

prune_in_volume() - to obtain a break-up of the number of vertices and segments present in each neuropil region.

I would suggest that you do

resample() e.g. to 1 or 0.5 µm step size to ensure that the neurons are evenly sampled.

For convenience there is a function in a package that was not formally released that should do what you want:

https://github.com/flyconnectome/tracerutils/blob/master/R/synapses_per_neuropil.R#L15

However this will be slow for many neurons. To speed things up, you could do something like the code below which uses some sample data available within nat and the JFRC2 space label field.

All the best,

Greg.

library(nat.flybrains)

# Get label field
# see https://github.com/VirtualFlyBrain/DrosAdultBRAINdomains for details
tf=tempfile(fileext = '.nrrd')
download.file('https://github.com/VirtualFlyBrain/DrosAdultBRAINdomains/blob/master/combinedIndexFiles/JFRCtempate2010.mask130819_Original.nrrd?raw=true', destfile = tf)
labelfield=read.im3d(tf)
# get integer id -> neuropil table
neuropils=read.table('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/VirtualFlyBrain/DrosAdultBRAINdomains/master/refData/Original_Index.tsv', sep="\t", header = T)

# Map points to correct space and onto label field using Cell07PNs neuronlist as an example
df=data.frame(neuron=rep(names(Cell07PNs), nvertices(Cell07PNs)))
df=cbind(df, xyzmatrix(Cell07PNs))
# you would use sample = FCWB for your points
dft=xform_brain(df, sample=IS2,ref=JFRC2)
jfrc2indices=coord2ind(xyzmatrix(dft), JFRC2)

# neuropil ids
ids=labelfield[jfrc2indices]
nptable=as.data.frame(table(ids))
merge(nptable, neuropils, by.y="Stack.id", by.x='ids',sort=F)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Greg and Gaspar,

Connector types are defined implicitly by their connections in CATMAID, i.e. a connector with a presynaptic and N postsynaptic links is considered a synaptic connector, one. And one that links treenodes using the `desmosome_with` relation is considered a desmosome connector. So far only some API endpoints support link types other than pre/post, mainly the ones needed to add and show them in the front-end (Connectivity Widget/Matrix, 3D, Graph, …). The particular API you linked to (`{project_id}/connector/skeleton`) is an example for an API that only knows synaptic connectors at the moment. I am happy to add this though and wonder what would be useful to you. I could imagine adding an optional parameter `allowed_link_types` to specify which skeletons to return. The most flexible would likely be a set of allowed link types. It's also what is done by some of the APIs that already know about other link types, like

https://catmaid.readthedocs.io/en/stable/_static/api/index.html#operation/skeletons_connectivity_create

The parameter basically is a set of incoming, outgoing, abutting, gapjunction, tightjunction, desmosome, attachment and close_object, defaulting to incoming an outgoing. This is the list of currently "known" link types, of which the API above accepts a list of `partner_reference` entries into:

https://github.com/catmaid/CATMAID/blob/ce1dee4485e76c3b33bc751d5440ce8477fb1f43/django/applications/catmaid/control/link.py#L16

Are there other APIs where such a parameter (or something similar) would be useful?

Cheers,
Tom

Hi Greg and Tom,

If the connector type was visible in natverse, we could build pipelines to look at the entire desmosomes graph or visualise desmosomes.
Currently we have to do it in three programs and it is a bit error prone and not so easily reproducible.

The two most important/common tasks would be to load skeletons with different connector types for visualisation and connectivity queries.

Currently if I load a skeleton from Catmaid that has both desmosomes and synapses, such as a muscle cell, in the 3d view I see blue - the synapses, and white - the desmosomes dots. It would be good if we could display these separately, say:

plot3d(Muscle_cell, WithConnectors = T, Connector_type = c("incoming", "outgoing", "abutting", "gapjunction", "tightjunction", "desmosome", "attachment", "close_object"))

but the different colours also tell me that natverse somehow sees that these are different connectors

another type of query where distinguishing connectors would be great is a get_connectors_between and similar query, for example

desmosomal_conn = catmaid_get_connectors_between(pre=presyn_skids, post=postsyn_skids, pid=11, Connector_type = c(...))

I can imagine that this would be very interesting also for nematode people where gap junction networks are an important part of the connectome analyses.

Best wishes,
Gaspar

messages.subject: Re: NBLAST with SWC file format
messages.body_plain:
Dear Evan,

Thanks for your interest in NBLAST. The NBLAST algorithm is of course not tied to a particular input file format. The natverse function read.neurons <https://natverse.org/nat/reference/read.neurons.html> can read in a set of SWC files (and a number of other file formats) to which you can then carry out NBLAST all by all clustering or other analyses:

library(natverse)
nl=read.neurons("/folder/of/swcs")

Then you need to convert to dotprops <https://natverse.org/nat/reference/dotprops.html> i.e. vector cloud format, minimally by doing:

nld=dotprops(nl)

And then you can follow the remaining steps of this tutorial:

http://natverse.org/nat.nblast/articles/NBLAST-Clustering.html

All the best,

Greg.

PS I have taken the liberty of ccing this message to the nat-user google group since the answer may be of interest to others.
